paragraphs: Dorothy lived in the middle of the great Kansas prairies, with Uncle Henry, who was a farmer, and Aunt Em, who was the farmer's wife. Their house was small, for the wood to build it had to be carried by wagon many miles. There were four walls, a floor and a roof, which made one room; and this room held a rusty looking cookstove, a cupboard for the dishes, a table, three or four chairs, and the beds. Uncle Henry and Aunt Em had a big bed in one corner, and Dorothy a little bed in another corner. There was no attic at all, and no cellar—except a small hole dug in the ground, called a cyclone cellar, where the family could go to stay safe if one of those great whirling windstorms came spinning across the land. It was reached by a trap door in the middle of the floor, from which a ladder led down into the small, dark hole.

When Dorothy stood in the doorway and looked around, she could see nothing but the great gray prairie on every side. Not a tree nor a house broke the wide sweep of flat country that reached to the edge of the sky in all directions. The sun had baked the plowed land into a gray mass, with little cracks running through it. Even the grass was not green, for the sun had burned the tops of the long blades until they were the same gray color to be seen everywhere. Once the house had been painted, but the sun bubbled up the paint and the rains washed it away, and now the house was as dull and gray as everything else.

When Aunt Em came there to live she was a young, pretty wife. The sun and wind had changed her, too. They had taken the sparkle from her eyes and left them a quiet gray; they had taken the red from her cheeks and lips, and they were gray also. She was thin and tired-looking, and never smiled now. When Dorothy first came to live with her, Aunt Em had been so surprised by the child's laughter that she would give a little jump and press her hand upon her heart whenever Dorothy's merry voice reached her ears; and she still looked at the little girl with wonder that she could find anything to laugh at.

Uncle Henry never laughed. He worked hard from morning till night and had almost forgotten what fun was. He was gray also, from his long beard to his rough boots, and he looked stern and serious, and hardly ever spoke.

It was Toto that made Dorothy laugh, and saved her from growing as gray as everything around her. Toto was not gray; he was a little black dog, with long silky hair and small black eyes that twinkled merrily on either side of his funny, wee nose. Toto played all day long, and Dorothy played with him, and loved him dearly.

Today, however, they were not playing. Uncle Henry sat upon the doorstep and looked worriedly at the sky, which was even grayer than usual. Dorothy stood in the door with Toto in her arms, and looked at the sky too. Aunt Em was washing the dishes.

From far away in the north they heard a low moan of the wind, and Uncle Henry and Dorothy could see where the long grass bowed in waves before the coming storm. Then came a sharp whistling in the air from the south, and as they turned their eyes that way they saw ripples in the grass coming from that direction also.
Suddenly Uncle Henry stood up.
"There's a cyclone coming, Em," he called to his wife. "I'll go look after the animals." Then he ran toward the sheds where the cows and horses were kept.
Aunt Em dropped her work and came to the door. One look told her the storm was very close.
"Quick, Dorothy!" she called. "Run for the cellar!"

Toto jumped out of Dorothy's arms and hid under the bed, and the girl went to get him. Aunt Em, in a great hurry, threw open the trap door in the floor and climbed down the ladder into the small, dark hole. Dorothy caught Toto at last and started to follow her aunt. When she was halfway across the room there came a great whoosh from the wind, and the house shook so hard that she lost her footing and sat down suddenly—plop!—upon the floor.
Then a strange thing happened.
The house whirled around two or three times and rose slowly through the air. Dorothy felt as if she were going up in a balloon.

The north wind and the south wind met right where the house stood, and made it the exact middle of the cyclone. In the middle of a cyclone the air is usually still, but the great push of the wind on every side of the house raised it up higher and higher, until it was at the very top of the cyclone; and there it stayed and was carried miles and miles away as easily as you could carry a feather.

It was very dark, and the wind whooshed and whistled all around her, but Dorothy found she was riding quite easily. After the first few whirls around, and one other time when the house tipped to one side, she felt as if she were being rocked gently, like a baby in a cradle.
Toto did not like it. He ran about the room, now here, now there, barking loudly; but Dorothy sat quite still on the floor and waited to see what would happen.

Once Toto got too near the open trap door, and fell in; and for a moment the little girl was very worried about him. But soon she saw one of his ears sticking up through the hole, for the strong push of the air was holding him up so that he could not fall. She crept to the hole, caught Toto by the ear, and pulled him carefully back into the room again, and then she closed the trap door so that no more accidents could happen.

Hour after hour went by, and slowly Dorothy stopped feeling frightened; but she felt quite lonely, and the wind whistled so loudly all about her that she could hardly hear anything else. At first she had wondered what would happen when the house came down again; but as the hours passed and nothing bad happened, she stopped worrying and decided to wait calmly and see what would come next. At last she crawled over the swaying floor to her bed, and lay down upon it; and Toto followed and curled up beside her.
In spite of the swaying of the house and the humming of the wind, Dorothy soon closed her eyes and fell fast asleep.

changeNotes.note: Para 1: cyclones described as whirling windstorms you shelter from, instead of winds 'mighty enough to crush any building in its path.'
Para 3: removed 'who was an orphan'; Dorothy simply 'first came to live with' Aunt Em.
Paras 3–4: Aunt Em's screaming at laughter softened to a little jump; Uncle Henry 'had almost forgotten what fun was' instead of not knowing joy.
Paras 7, 10–12: storm sounds and alarm toned down (wail→moan, shriek→whoosh, 'screamed'→'called', 'badly frightened'→'in a great hurry').
Para 16: 'the wind howled horribly' became whooshing and whistling; the house 'tipped to one side' rather than 'tipped badly.'
Para 18: Dorothy is 'worried' rather than thinking she had lost Toto; she pulls him back carefully instead of dragging him by the ear.
Para 19: removed fear of being 'dashed to pieces' and nearly going deaf; she wonders what will happen when the house comes down.
Swapped harder words for a 5-year-old listener: garret→attic, lumber→wood, stock→animals, gaunt→tired-looking, sober→quiet, solemn→serious, blistered→bubbled up, pressure→push, resolved→decided.

paragraphs: The soldier with the green whiskers led them through the streets of the Emerald City until they reached the room where the Guardian of the Gates lived. This officer unlocked their green spectacles to put them back in his great box, and then he politely opened the gate for our friends.
“Which road leads to the Wicked Witch of the West?” asked Dorothy.
“There is no road,” answered the Guardian of the Gates. “No one ever wishes to go that way.”
“How, then, are we to find her?” asked the girl.
“That will be easy,” replied the man, “for when she knows you are in the country of the Winkies she will find you, and make you all work for her as her servants.”
“Perhaps not,” said the Scarecrow, “for we mean to stop her.”

“Oh, that is different,” said the Guardian of the Gates. “No one has ever stopped her before, so I naturally thought she would make you work for her, as she does all the rest. But take care; for she is wicked and fierce, and may not let you stop her. Keep to the West, where the sun sets, and you cannot fail to find her.”

They thanked him and said good-bye, and turned toward the West, walking over fields of soft grass dotted here and there with daisies and buttercups. Dorothy still wore the pretty silk dress she had put on in the palace, but now, to her surprise, she found it was no longer green, but pure white. The ribbon around Toto’s neck had also lost its green color and was as white as Dorothy’s dress.

The Emerald City was soon left far behind. As they went on, the ground became rougher and hillier, for there were no farms nor houses in this country of the West, and no one had ever planted anything there.

In the afternoon the sun shone hot in their faces, for there were no trees to give them shade; so that before night Dorothy and Toto and the Lion were tired, and lay down upon the grass and fell asleep, with the Woodman and the Scarecrow keeping watch.

Now the Wicked Witch of the West had only one eye, yet that eye could see as far as a telescope, the kind of tube that lets you see things very far away, and it could see everywhere. So, as she sat in the door of her castle, she happened to look around and saw Dorothy lying asleep, with Toto and her friends all about her. They were a long way off, but the Wicked Witch was cross to find them in her country; so she blew upon a silver whistle that hung around her neck.
At once there came running to her from all directions a pack of great wolves. They had long legs and gleaming eyes and big, grumbly growls.
“Go to those people,” said the Witch, “and chase them out of my country.”
“Are you not going to make them work for you?” asked the leader of the wolves.
“No,” she answered, “one is of tin, and one of straw; one is a girl and another a Lion. None of them is fit to work, so you may chase them off.”
“Very well,” said the wolf, and he dashed away at full speed, followed by the others.
It was lucky the Scarecrow and the Woodman were wide awake and heard the wolves coming.
“This is my job,” said the Woodman, “so get behind me and I will meet them as they come.”

He took up his axe, which he kept very bright and shiny, and as the leader of the wolves came on, the Tin Woodman swung it about so bravely, clanging and flashing in the sun, that the wolf gave a yelp and ran away as fast as he could go. As soon as the Woodman could raise his axe again another wolf came up, and he too took one look at that flashing axe and ran. There were forty wolves, and forty times a wolf turned tail, until at last they were all running off over the hills with their tails tucked between their legs.
Then he put down his axe and sat beside the Scarecrow, who said, “That was well done, friend. I would have helped, but I was busy thinking.”

They waited until Dorothy awoke the next morning. The little girl was quite surprised when she saw so many big paw prints all over the grass, and Toto sniffed at every one of them, but the Tin Woodman told her all. She thanked him for keeping them safe and sat down to breakfast, after which they started again upon their journey.

Now this same morning the Wicked Witch came to the door of her castle and looked out with her one eye that could see far off. She saw all her wolves hiding in their dens, and the strangers still traveling through her country. This made her crosser than before, and she blew her silver whistle twice.
Right away a great flock of wild crows came flying toward her, so many that they made the sky look dark.
And the Wicked Witch said to the King Crow, “Fly at once to the strangers; peck at them and chase them away.”
The wild crows flew in one great flock toward Dorothy and her friends. When the little girl saw them coming she was afraid, and Toto barked and barked.
But the Scarecrow said, “This is my turn, so lie down beside me and you will be quite safe.”

So they all lay upon the ground, with Dorothy holding Toto close, except the Scarecrow, and he stood up and stretched out his arms. And when the crows saw him they were frightened, as these birds always are by scarecrows, and did not dare to come any nearer. But the King Crow said:
“It is only a stuffed man. I am not afraid of him!”

The King Crow flew at the Scarecrow, who caught it by its tail feathers and gave it such a shake that it squawked and flapped away as fast as its wings could carry it. And then another crow flew at him, and the Scarecrow shook that one too. There were forty crows, and forty times the Scarecrow gave a crow a good shake, until at last every one of them had flown away home, squawking and ruffled, leaving only a few black feathers on the grass. Then he called to his friends to get up, and again they went upon their journey.
When the Wicked Witch looked out again and saw all her crows hiding in their nests with their feathers in a muddle, she got into a terrible temper, and blew three times upon her silver whistle.
Right away there was heard a great buzzing in the air, and a swarm of black bees came flying toward her.

“Go to the strangers and sting them!” commanded the Witch, and the bees turned and flew quickly until they came to where Dorothy and her friends were walking. But the Woodman had seen them coming, and the Scarecrow had decided what to do.

“Take out my straw and scatter it over the little girl and the dog and the Lion,” he said to the Woodman, “and the bees cannot sting them.” This the Woodman did, and as Dorothy lay close beside the Lion and held Toto in her arms, the straw covered them all up.

The bees came and found no one but the Woodman to sting, so they flew at him and bumped their stings against the tin, without hurting the Woodman at all. Bonk, bonk, bonk! went the bees, until their stings were all bent and they were so dizzy that they tumbled down around the Woodman in little heaps, like heaps of fine black coal. And when at last they could fly again, they buzzed slowly off home, grumbling all the way.

Then Dorothy and the Lion got up, and Toto shook the straw out of his fur, and the girl helped the Tin Woodman put the straw back into the Scarecrow again, until he was as good as ever. So they started upon their journey once more.

The Wicked Witch was so angry when she saw her black bees tumbled in little heaps like fine coal that she stamped her foot and pulled at her hair and ground her teeth. And then she called a dozen of her servants, who were the Winkies, and told them to go to the strangers and chase them away.

The Winkies were not a brave people, but they had to do as they were told. So they marched away until they came near to Dorothy. Then the Lion gave a great roar and leaped towards them, and the poor Winkies were so frightened that they ran back as fast as they could.

When they returned to the castle the Wicked Witch scolded them very crossly, and sent them back to their work, after which she sat down to think what she should do next. She could not understand how all her plans to stop these strangers had failed; but she was a powerful Witch, as well as a wicked one, and she soon made up her mind what to do.

changeNotes.note: References to slaves and making the travelers slaves were changed to servants or being made to work for the Witch (paragraphs 5, 7, 14, 36).
Removed the threats to 'destroy' the Witch and to 'tear them to pieces' or 'peck out their eyes'. The Witch's orders are now to chase or drive the travelers away, and the friends mean to 'stop' her.
The Tin Woodman no longer kills forty wolves with his axe. His flashing, clanging axe scares them off, and the pile of wolves becomes paw prints. The later plot does not depend on the wolves dying.

The Scarecrow no longer twists the necks of forty crows. He shakes each one by the tail feathers and it flies away home. The Witch now sees her crows hiding in their nests instead of a heap of dead birds.

The bees no longer die when their stings break. Their stings bend against the tin and they tumble down dizzy in little heaps like fine coal, then buzz off home. The coal image is kept for the Witch's reaction.
Removed the sharp spears given to the Winkies and the 'sting them to death' order.
The Witch beating the Winkies with a strap was replaced with her scolding them crossly.
The wolves' 'fierce eyes and sharp teeth' became 'gleaming eyes and big, grumbly growls'. The Witch is 'cross' rather than 'angry' in places, and her rage is described as a temper.
The King Crow's taunt 'I will peck his eyes out' became 'I am not afraid of him!' The Witch 'pulled at' rather than 'tore' her hair.

Swapped hard words for easier ones: 'inquired' became 'asked', 'untilled' became 'no one had ever planted anything', 'Straightway/Forthwith' became 'Right away', 'bade him good-bye' became 'said good-bye'. Added short explanations of 'spectacles' (green) and 'telescope'.

Gave Toto small moments in the scenes he is in: sniffing paw prints, barking at the crows, being held close, shaking out straw. Added a light joke for the Scarecrow ('I was busy thinking') to keep the friends funny.

changeNotes.note: Replaced talk of making people 'slaves' with being made to work for the Witch and never let go (paragraphs 5, 7, 14, 15, 36).
Changed the Witch's orders to 'tear them to pieces' into 'get rid of them' and similar milder commands.
The Woodman still defeats all forty wolves, but the beheading is not described; the wolves simply fall and lie still.
Removed the order to 'peck out their eyes'; the crows are told to peck at and drive off the travelers.
The Scarecrow still defeats all forty crows, but the neck-twisting is described only as 'a quick twist' with no mention of dying.
Changed 'sting them to death' to 'sting them'.
The Witch beating the Winkies with a strap is now 'was very cruel to them and punished them,' without showing the beating.

paragraphs: Dorothy lived in the middle of the great Kansas prairies, with Uncle Henry, who was a farmer, and Aunt Em, who was the farmer’s wife. Their house was small, for the lumber to build it had to be carried by wagon many miles. There were four walls, a floor and a roof, which made one room; and this room held a rusty looking cookstove, a cupboard for the dishes, a table, three or four chairs, and the beds. Uncle Henry and Aunt Em had a big bed in one corner, and Dorothy a little bed in another corner. There was no attic at all, and no cellar—except a small hole dug in the ground, called a cyclone cellar, where the family could go in case one of those great whirlwinds arose, mighty enough to crush any building in its path. It was reached by a trap door in the middle of the floor, from which a ladder led down into the small, dark hole.

When Dorothy stood in the doorway and looked around, she could see nothing but the great gray prairie on every side. Not a tree nor a house broke the broad sweep of flat country that reached to the edge of the sky in all directions. The sun had baked the plowed land into a gray mass, with little cracks running through it. Even the grass was not green, for the sun had burned the tops of the long blades until they were the same gray color to be seen everywhere. Once the house had been painted, but the sun blistered the paint and the rains washed it away, and now the house was as dull and gray as everything else.

When Aunt Em came there to live she was a young, pretty wife. The sun and wind had changed her, too. They had taken the sparkle from her eyes and left them a serious gray; they had taken the red from her cheeks and lips, and they were gray also. She was thin and worn, and never smiled now. When Dorothy, who was an orphan, first came to her, Aunt Em had been so startled by the child’s laughter that she would scream and press her hand upon her heart whenever Dorothy’s merry voice reached her ears; and she still looked at the little girl with wonder that she could find anything to laugh at.

Uncle Henry never laughed. He worked hard from morning till night and did not know what joy was. He was gray also, from his long beard to his rough boots, and he looked stern and serious, and rarely spoke.

It was Toto that made Dorothy laugh, and saved her from growing as gray as everything else around her. Toto was not gray; he was a little black dog, with long silky hair and small black eyes that twinkled merrily on either side of his funny, wee nose. Toto played all day long, and Dorothy played with him, and loved him dearly.

Today, however, they were not playing. Uncle Henry sat upon the doorstep and looked anxiously at the sky, which was even grayer than usual. Dorothy stood in the door with Toto in her arms, and looked at the sky too. Aunt Em was washing the dishes.

From the far north they heard a low wail of the wind, and Uncle Henry and Dorothy could see where the long grass bowed in waves before the coming storm. There now came a sharp whistling in the air from the south, and as they turned their eyes that way they saw ripples in the grass coming from that direction also.
Suddenly Uncle Henry stood up.
“There’s a cyclone coming, Em,” he called to his wife. “I’ll go look after the stock.” Then he ran toward the sheds where the cows and horses were kept.
Aunt Em dropped her work and came to the door. One glance told her that danger was close at hand.
“Quick, Dorothy!” she screamed. “Run for the cellar!”

Toto jumped out of Dorothy’s arms and hid under the bed, and the girl started to get him. Aunt Em, badly frightened, threw open the trap door in the floor and climbed down the ladder into the small, dark hole. Dorothy caught Toto at last and started to follow her aunt. When she was halfway across the room there came a great shriek from the wind, and the house shook so hard that she lost her footing and sat down suddenly upon the floor.
Then a strange thing happened.
The house whirled around two or three times and rose slowly through the air. Dorothy felt as if she were going up in a balloon.

The north and south winds met where the house stood, and made it the exact center of the cyclone. In the middle of a cyclone the air is usually still. But the great push of the wind on every side of the house raised it up higher and higher, until it was at the very top of the cyclone; and there it stayed and was carried miles and miles away as easily as you could carry a feather.

It was very dark, and the wind howled horribly around her, but Dorothy found she was riding quite easily. After the first few whirls around, and one other time when the house tipped badly, she felt as if she were being rocked gently, like a baby in a cradle.
Toto did not like it. He ran about the room, now here, now there, barking loudly; but Dorothy sat quite still on the floor and waited to see what would happen.

Once Toto got too near the open trap door, and fell in; and at first the little girl thought she had lost him. But soon she saw one of his ears sticking up through the hole, for the strong push of the air was keeping him up so that he could not fall. She crept to the hole, caught Toto by the ear, and dragged him into the room again, and then closed the trap door so that no more accidents could happen.

Hour after hour passed away, and slowly Dorothy got over her fright; but she felt quite lonely, and the wind shrieked so loudly all about her that she nearly went deaf. At first she had wondered if she would be dashed to pieces when the house fell again; but as the hours passed and nothing terrible happened, she stopped worrying and decided to wait calmly and see what the future would bring. At last she crawled over the swaying floor to her bed, and lay down upon it; and Toto followed and lay down beside her.
In spite of the swaying of the house and the wailing of the wind, Dorothy soon closed her eyes and fell fast asleep.

changeNotes.note: Swapped a few old-fashioned or harder words for easier ones ("midst" to "middle," "garret" to "attic," "contained" to "held," "sober" and "solemn" to "serious," "gaunt" to "worn," "resolved" to "decided").
Explained the cyclone's lifting force more simply ("pressure" to "push") and split one long sentence in paragraph 15.
Lightly reworded a few phrases for easier reading ("her other surroundings" to "everything else around her," "told her of the danger" to "told her that danger was").

paragraphs: The soldier with the green whiskers led them through the streets of the Emerald City until they reached the room where the Guardian of the Gates lived. This officer unlocked their spectacles to put them back in his great box, and then he politely opened the gate for our friends.
“Which road leads to the Wicked Witch of the West?” asked Dorothy.
“There is no road,” answered the Guardian of the Gates. “No one ever wishes to go that way.”
“How, then, are we to find her?” asked the girl.
“That will be easy,” replied the man, “for when she knows you are in the country of the Winkies she will find you, and make you all work for her as her servants.”
“Perhaps not,” said the Scarecrow, “for we mean to destroy her.”

“Oh, that is different,” said the Guardian of the Gates. “No one has ever destroyed her before, so I naturally thought she would make servants of you, as she has of the rest. But take care; for she is wicked and fierce, and may not allow you to destroy her. Keep to the West, where the sun sets, and you cannot fail to find her.”

They thanked him and said good-bye, and turned toward the West, walking over fields of soft grass dotted here and there with daisies and buttercups. Dorothy still wore the pretty silk dress she had put on in the palace, but now, to her surprise, she found it was no longer green, but pure white. The ribbon around Toto’s neck had also lost its green color and was as white as Dorothy’s dress.
The Emerald City was soon left far behind. As they went on, the ground became rougher and hillier, for there were no farms nor houses in this country of the West, and no one had ever plowed the land.

In the afternoon the sun shone hot in their faces, for there were no trees to offer them shade; so that before night Dorothy and Toto and the Lion were tired, and lay down upon the grass and fell asleep, with the Woodman and the Scarecrow keeping watch.

Now the Wicked Witch of the West had only one eye, yet that was as powerful as a telescope, and could see everywhere. So, as she sat in the door of her castle, she happened to look around and saw Dorothy lying asleep, with her friends all about her. They were a long distance off, but the Wicked Witch was angry to find them in her country; so she blew upon a silver whistle that hung around her neck.
At once there came running to her from all directions a pack of great wolves. They had long legs and fierce eyes and sharp teeth.
“Go to those people,” said the Witch, “and destroy them.”
“Are you not going to make them your servants?” asked the leader of the wolves.
“No,” she answered, “one is of tin, and one of straw; one is a girl and another a Lion. None of them is fit to work, so you may destroy them all.”
“Very well,” said the wolf, and he dashed away at full speed, followed by the others.
It was lucky the Scarecrow and the Woodman were wide awake and heard the wolves coming.
“This is my fight,” said the Woodman, “so get behind me and I will meet them as they come.”

He seized his axe, which he had made very sharp, and as the leader of the wolves came on, the Tin Woodman swung his arm with one mighty blow, and the wolf fell and did not get up again. As soon as he could raise his axe another wolf came up, and he also fell before the Tin Woodman’s axe. There were forty wolves, and forty times a wolf fell, so that at last they all lay still in a heap before the Woodman.
Then he put down his axe and sat beside the Scarecrow, who said, “It was a good fight, friend.”

They waited until Dorothy awoke the next morning. The little girl was quite frightened when she saw the great pile of shaggy wolves, but the Tin Woodman told her all. She thanked him for saving them and sat down to breakfast, after which they started again upon their journey.

Now this same morning the Wicked Witch came to the door of her castle and looked out with her one eye that could see far off. She saw all her wolves lying still and defeated, and the strangers still traveling through her country. This made her angrier than before, and she blew her silver whistle twice.
Right away a great flock of wild crows came flying toward her, enough to darken the sky.
And the Wicked Witch said to the King Crow, “Fly at once to the strangers; peck at them and drive them to their ruin.”
The wild crows flew in one great flock toward Dorothy and her companions. When the little girl saw them coming she was afraid.
But the Scarecrow said, “This is my battle, so lie down beside me and you will not be harmed.”

So they all lay upon the ground except the Scarecrow, and he stood up and stretched out his arms. And when the crows saw him they were frightened, as these birds always are by scarecrows, and did not dare to come any nearer. But the King Crow said:
“It is only a stuffed man. I will peck his eyes out.”

The King Crow flew at the Scarecrow, who caught it by the head and gave it a quick twist, and it dropped to the ground and lay still. And then another crow flew at him, and the Scarecrow did the same to it. There were forty crows, and forty times the Scarecrow caught one, until at last all were lying still beside him. Then he called to his companions to rise, and again they went upon their journey.
When the Wicked Witch looked out again and saw all her crows lying in a heap, she got into a terrible rage, and blew three times upon her silver whistle.
At once there was heard a great buzzing in the air, and a swarm of black bees came flying toward her.

“Go to the strangers and sting them until they can go no further!” commanded the Witch, and the bees turned and flew rapidly until they came to where Dorothy and her friends were walking. But the Woodman had seen them coming, and the Scarecrow had decided what to do.

“Take out my straw and scatter it over the little girl and the dog and the Lion,” he said to the Woodman, “and the bees cannot sting them.” This the Woodman did, and as Dorothy lay close beside the Lion and held Toto in her arms, the straw covered them entirely.

The bees came and found no one but the Woodman to sting, so they flew at him and broke off all their stings against the tin, without hurting the Woodman at all. And as bees cannot live when their stings are broken, that was the end of the black bees, and they lay scattered thick about the Woodman, like little heaps of fine coal.
Then Dorothy and the Lion got up, and the girl helped the Tin Woodman put the straw back into the Scarecrow again, until he was as good as ever. So they started upon their journey once more.

The Wicked Witch was so angry when she saw her black bees in little heaps like fine coal that she stamped her foot and tore her hair and gnashed her teeth. And then she called a dozen of her servants, who were the Winkies, and gave them sharp spears, telling them to go to the strangers and destroy them.

The Winkies were not a brave people, but they had to do as they were told. So they marched away until they came near to Dorothy. Then the Lion gave a great roar and sprang towards them, and the poor Winkies were so frightened that they ran back as fast as they could.

When they returned to the castle the Wicked Witch punished them harshly, and sent them back to their work, after which she sat down to think what she should do next. She could not understand how all her plans to destroy these strangers had failed; but she was a powerful Witch, as well as a wicked one, and she soon made up her mind how to act.

changeNotes.note: Changed 'slaves' to 'servants' throughout (paragraphs 5, 7, 14, 36), keeping the idea that the Witch forces people to work for her.
The Witch's orders to 'tear them to pieces' / 'tear them into small pieces' became 'destroy them' (paragraphs 13, 15).
The Tin Woodman no longer chops off the wolf's head; the wolves fall to one mighty blow and lie still in a heap (paragraph 19).
Wolves and crows are described as 'lying still' or 'defeated' rather than 'dead' (paragraphs 19, 22, 29). They are still defeated for good.
The Witch's command to 'peck out their eyes and tear them to pieces' became 'peck at them and drive them to their ruin' (paragraph 24). The King Crow's boast about the stuffed man's eyes was kept.
The Scarecrow gives each crow a quick twist instead of twisting its neck until it dies (paragraph 29).
'Sting them to death' became 'sting them until they can go no further' (paragraph 32). The bees' end was kept as the author wrote it.
The Witch beating the Winkies with a strap became 'punished them harshly' (paragraph 38).

Replaced a few old-fashioned words with simpler ones: 'inquired' to 'asked', 'bade him good-bye' to 'said good-bye', 'untilled' to 'no one had ever plowed the land', 'advanced' to 'went on', 'had but one eye' to 'had only one eye', and 'Straightway'/'Forthwith' to 'Right away'/'At once'.
